_what: D191 register note on kvflow-prefetch: the DRY port-rule count must not be cited as the arm's LIVE prefetch rate. Raised by the H100 from the first live cell and recorded here rather than by editing either the gated cell list or the dry proof, so each number keeps its own register and provenance.
why_this_note_exists: The gated KVFLOW_CELLS header and d187_kvflow_prefetch_posted_proofs.json both report a DRY measurement: 108 prefetch_ahead decisions against the base kvflow's 9, so 99 attributable, matching the arm's own prefetch_ahead_emitted of 99. That is a correct PORT-RULE proof, which asks only whether the characteristic decision occurs at least once. It is NOT a rate, and the header's unexpressible figure (19,107 against 99 emitted, 0.5 percent expressed) is a DRY figure that a reader could easily carry into a sentence about the live system.

dry_OBSERVED_on_a_dry_cell.source: d187_kvflow_prefetch_posted_proofs.json, dry seed-4 cell, posted knobs
dry_OBSERVED_on_a_dry_cell.register: OBSERVED count of decision rows on a DRY cell; a port-rule existence proof

live_OBSERVED_on_the_s4_cell.register: OBSERVED counters from a LIVE cell; this is the rate, the dry figure is not

the_correction: The live mechanism is about 16x more active than the dry proof suggested: 8.3 percent of asks expressed live against 0.5 percent dry. The likely reason, offered as the H100's reading and not as a measured cause, is that live sessions and real engine telemetry put more sessions in the expressible state than a dry cell does. SO: cite 1,628 and 8.3 percent for the live arm, and 99 only as the port-rule existence proof.
the_caveat_that_still_stands: 92 percent of asks remain UNEXPRESSIBLE live (17,954 of 19,582), so kvflow-prefetch is still NOT the published system at full strength and must not be reported as such. The direction of the correction matters: it makes the arm look MORE active, so it weakens any claim that the port passed on a technicality, and it does not weaken the not-at-full-strength caveat at all.

also_recorded_about_this_cell.note_on_by_deadline: equal to the cell's own floor
also_recorded_about_this_cell.D144_2_check: 23 errors of 9,358 requests is 0.25 percent, well under D144 (2)'s 5 percent saturation-labelling threshold, so the run is NOT labelled saturated by the ERROR rule. It is saturated on LOAD and on sitting at its own floor, which is a different and weaker statement and should be written as such.
also_recorded_about_this_cell.floor_caveat: an arm AT its floor orders against other arms uninformatively, the same caveat already attached to lmcache s6 at 0.083 against a 0.058 floor

null_status_requests_RESOLVED.query_type: all 23 are DASHCAM monitors; none robot or assistance
null_status_requests_RESOLVED.WHY_THIS_MATTERS: Unlike lmcache s6, where both null-status requests already carried cloud_payload.on_time FALSE and the fix changed nothing, TWO of these 23 were flagged ON TIME by the coordinator. So D175 (1) REMOVED two on-time dashcam deliveries that would otherwise have FLATTERED a published baseline. The scorer's pooled dashcam 0.069 already excludes them.
null_status_requests_RESOLVED.consequence_for_the_design_log: D175 (1) records 'measured impact on committed numbers is zero'. That statement was TRUE for the cells committed when it was written and is NOT a claim that the guard is inert. This is the FIRST measured instance of it changing a number: 2 deliveries on kvflow-prefetch s4. The log entry should not be read as 'the refusal path never bites', and any future cell must be scored with the guard rather than on the assumption that it is a no-op.
null_status_requests_RESOLVED.generalisation_tested: the confirmation now rests on 23 requests across a saturated arm, not on the 2 of the lmcache case, which is why it was worth checking rather than assuming
